title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). The experiment used a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine). A single shared initial candidate was generated per task by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120). A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks and triggered ≤1 repair only when validator.violation_count>0. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120 (1.00); guarded success = 120/120 (1.00). Contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Validator traces show repair_applied=false for all guarded episodes. We incorporated reviewer-requested clarifications: shared-generation semantics, repair-trigger logic, and an artifact-grounded explanation of the degenerate statistical outcome. We expand methodology, execution accounting, representative diagnostics, reproducibility guidance, and limitations grounded in the archived artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can synthesize human-readable network configuration commands from natural-language intent, enabling faster NetOps workflows. However, plausible-looking commands may violate workflow constraints (for example, requiring shutdown before MTU changes or make‑before‑break ordering for uplink switchover), produce regressions, or break operational invariants. Prior work therefore proposes adding formal verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers to LLM-driven pipelines so that generated candidates are checked and, where necessary, repaired before enactment. Evaluating such guarded pipelines requires closed‑loop executable tests that expose semantic/network‑level failures beyond token- or syntax‑level correctness. We designed a preregistered paired experiment to answer a focused mechanistic question: does inserting an executable emulator validator and a single-step repair mechanism change semantic failure outcomes when both conditions receive the same generated candidate?

The confirmatory research question (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) asked: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects from generation variance we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: the same generation was presented to both conditions for each task so any difference must arise from the validator/repair stage acting on identical outputs. The present paper reports the preregistered design, exact execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, per‑topology summaries, representative validator traces, and an artifact-grounded interpretation of the degenerate ceiling outcome observed in the run.
sections.related_work:
Evaluations that stop at generated text correctness miss operational failure modes exposed only by closed‑loop execution. Recent executable benchmarks and testbeds (e.g., NetConfArena and other digital‑twin efforts) emphasize closed‑loop assessment of agentic NetOps behaviors and show that generate→validate→repair architectures can reduce semantic errors in constrained settings. Tool and survey papers additionally recommend guardrails such as veto layers, canary deployments, translation to formal models, and external validators to mitigate unsafe automated actions.

Those prior studies typically evaluate multi-component systems where generator variance, prompt engineering, and integration differences confound attribution. Our experiment complements those works by holding generator outputs constant and isolating the validator/repair marginal effect on identical candidates. This separation is methodologically important because it clarifies whether a validator provides benefit independent of generator errors; however, it also narrows generality because real deployments will usually present generation variability, adversarial prompts, and multiple model families.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: We preregistered the study (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) and archived the manifest before execution. The preregistered design specified a paired binary outcome on N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks, deterministically assigned to three topology classes (40 tasks each: edge, core, leaf–spine). For each task a single shared initial candidate was to be generated by a declared hosted model (gpt-5-mini) and delivered unchanged to both conditions; the preregistration explicitly set independent_condition_generation=false to enforce the shared‑generation pairing.

Generation stage and model configuration: The run used the declared model requested_model: "gpt-5-mini" with parameters recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. The execution manifest shows model_calls_used = 120 and stage accounting records shared_initial_generation = 120. The shared-generation stage ensures that any downstream difference arises only from the validator/repair interaction with identical produced text rather than generation variance.

Validator and repair semantics: The guarded pipeline integrated a deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, validator_version = 5.0). The validator executed intent-constraint checks and workflow‑policy rules encoded in the task payloads (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break patterns). Its scoring rule was labeled full_intent_constraint_validation and it produced structured validator_trace artifacts containing fields validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. Per the preregistered repair policy, a repair iteration could be invoked at most once and only when validator.violation_count>0; repair prompts and repair_provider_trace artifacts were to be archived if used.

Task generation and difficulty metadata: The task bank was produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task manifest entry encodes constraints, an explicit required_sequence describing correct ordering of field changes (for example, shut→mtu→vlan→up), initial_state, expected_final_state, and difficulty tags (medium/hard/very_hard) with dependency_rule_count and required_command_count. These metadata enable stratified post-hoc analyses and reproduce the exact operational constraints the validator enforces.

Confirmatory estimand and inferential plan: The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (the per-pair reduction in emulator-observed semantic-failure probability). The preregistered confirmatory test was the exact two‑sided McNemar; complementary reporting included the paired difference and a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples and bootstrap_seed = 1729 (both archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The primary analysis used complete_pairs only; preregistered sensitivity analyses would treat technical exclusions as failures if needed.

Instrumentation, contamination controls, and accounting: The execution harness recorded provider-call audit logs and enforced a deterministic emulator-state reset between tasks (container image checks and deterministic seeds). Contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache‑key reuse) were applied and logged; none triggered exclusions. The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts provide full episode accounting. All raw provider traces, responses, scorer JSONs, and analysis artifacts were archived to permit independent verification.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes: The run completed the planned episodes: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, model_calls_used = 120. analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline = 120 successes, 0 failures and guarded = 120 successes, 0 failures (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. analysis/missingness_summary.csv shows complete_pairs = 120 and zero technical/instrumentation exclusions; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty.

Confirmatory statistics: Because the contingency table contained zero discordant pairs, the exact two‑sided McNemar p‑value equals 1.0 and the paired-difference estimate is 0.00. The preregistered bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) returned [0.00, 0.00]. This degenerate, zero‑width CI arises because resampling from an empirical paired distribution with no discordant pairs reproduces identical paired outcomes across resamples; the archived analysis_log.jsonl records the bootstrap parameters and the completed paired analysis event.

Per‑topology aggregated results: Tasks were deterministically assigned 40 per topology class. Per-topology aggregated success counts from archived artifacts are:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
These counts are directly supported by the task_manifest.jsonl entries and the scoring JSONs in execution/scoring/; representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json etc.) show normalized_response matching normalized_reference_answer and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true.

Representative validator diagnostics: Representative scoring JSONs in the archive demonstrate the validator's structured outputs. For example, execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json records parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 4, observed_touched_field_count = 3, validator_trace.validation_after.normalized_configuration matching the expected sequence, validator_trace.violation_count = 0, and validator_trace.repair_applied = false. Similar artifacts exist for varied difficulty patterns (paired_link_atomic_mtu_change, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, rolling_access_vlan_migration), illustrating that the validator exercised dependency checks and per‑task difficulty metadata even when no violations occurred.

Repair activity and vacuous secondary outcomes: Per the preregistered repair policy repairs are conditional on validator.violation_count>0. Because violation_count = 0 for every guarded episode, repair_applied = false across the archive and no repair_provider_trace artifacts were generated. Consequently, preregistered secondary endpoints such as proportion of tasks requiring repair and mean repair calls per successful task are vacuous for this run.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling/null outcome: The shared-generation pairing intentionally removed generator variance so that any observed difference would come solely from the validator/repair stage operating on identical candidates. In this task bank, the shared initial candidates produced by gpt-5-mini satisfied the deterministic emulator validator's encoded intent constraints and workflow policies, yielding a concordant-success ceiling (n_11 = 120). Under these conditions the guarded pipeline could not exercise repair behavior and therefore could not reduce semantic failures relative to baseline. The exact McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical manifestations of this ceiling and are artifact‑grounded in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.

Methodological implications and boundary interpretation: The paired shared‑generation design answers a precise mechanistic question — whether a validator/repair stage can improve outcomes for identical generator outputs — and the answer in this curated synthetic task bank and under the archived generator/prompting is "no effect" because the generator produced only valid candidates. This narrow null should not be interpreted as evidence that validators are unnecessary in broader settings. In practice, generator variance, adversarial prompts, prompt perturbations, other model families, or operational heterogeneity may produce invalid candidates for which a validator/repair subsystem could be decisive. The archived artifacts (task_manifest.jsonl, execution/scoring/*.json) enable future researchers to relax the shared-generation constraint and rerun with independent per‑condition generations to empirically measure repair utility under realistic generation variability.

Design recommendations supported by artifacts: To measure practical repair utility, confirmatory designs should permit independent per‑condition generation so that the guard can act on generator errors. Other favourable design changes include increasing the repair budget beyond a single iteration, testing multiple generator models and prompt perturbation schemes, and adding multi‑vendor behavioral models to the validator. The archived task metadata (difficulty tags, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) supports stratified study designs that can focus on high‑dependency or high‑transience task classes where validators are more likely to be beneficial.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity — prompt sensitivity and shared-generation choices are deliberate design decisions; the run records independent_condition_generation=false and one shared_initial_generation per pair. Construct validity — the deterministic emulator validator operationalizes semantic correctness according to explicit task payload workflow policies; this reproducible formalization trades some production realism for deterministic scoring. External validity — tasks are synthetic and deterministic, limiting generalization to heterogeneous, multi‑vendor production networks. Conclusion validity — the preregistered power assumption targeted an absolute reduction of 0.15 but was unattainable because baseline succeeded on the entire task set; the archive documents this mismatch (preregistration power_and_precision_plan and analysis artifacts).

Operational implications and auditability: Even though the validator was unused here, the archive shows how deterministic validator traces can support operator audit and post-hoc analysis. Validator outputs include per‑task fields showing which rules passed/failed, parsed command and touched‑field counts, and an explicit repair_applied flag; these structured traces are suitable for operator-facing explanations and for constructing independent audit trails. The execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation artifacts demonstrate reproducible provider audit logs and deterministic reset checks required for accountable automated NetOps runs.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator; the run produced n_11 = 120 (baseline and guarded successes), a paired-difference estimate of 0.00, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and a bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling effect for this curated synthetic task bank and clarifies that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our main contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and provide deterministic archival artifacts (model configuration, task manifest, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts) so that future studies can relax pairing constraints, test multiple models and prompt perturbations, and evaluate richer repair budgets against more production-rooted corpora.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi‑vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation‑variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi‑vendor, partially observable production environments; some real‑world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
